en: Abhidhānottara 22. [Tib. 25] = NGMPP E 1517/7 964– = Lokesh Chandra pp. 158–167.
Now I shall further proclaim the path of yoga, which is very difficult to attain—
the heart of the yoga of the Yoginīs, the sequential yoga of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Instantly arisen from the syllable, instantly marked by the insignia,
Vajrasattva is indeed the supreme bliss of great bliss.
Having undergone the transformation of that [nature], one instantly becomes the supreme Heruka,
resembling the autumn sky and like the *atasī* flower.
Eight-armed and four-faced, the inspirer of fear even in fear itself,
seated in the *ālīḍha* posture, three-eyed, the Lord of Yoginīs.
White on the left and red on the other [right] side, with a beautiful yellow face above,
the Hero wears a garland of skulls and is empowered by the five mudrās.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
he stands upon the lotus feet of Bhairava and Kālarātri.
Embraced by the Vajra-bell, she is Vārāhī with her knees encircled;
she has attained the non-dual yoga, with disheveled hair and naked.
She has a girdle adorned with pieces [of jewels] resembling her own complexion,
bears the marks of his face and arms, and is graced by the perfection of yoga.
He holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, wears a garment of elephant hide, and possesses two arms;
he carries a mallet, a trident, and a battle-axe, while the eighth is a human head of Brahmā.
Wearing a crescent moon, peaceful, adorned with a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra),
his body decorated with the six mudrās, and graced by the vajra insignia.
The crown bears a garland of vajras, while the girdle and anklets resound;
the armlets are marked with vajras.
Such is the heart-mantra, the leader of mantras;
[it depicts] Vārāhī seated comfortably, adorned with the skin of a Jina.
And the *ḍamaru* [is the emblem] of Vārāhī;
the Blessed One, bearing his own emblem, is in the center of the pericarp upon an eight-petalled, delightful,
and beautiful lotus with petals of various colors— the most excellent among all the Buddhas.
One should place four Ḍākinīs in the cardinal directions beginning with the eastern petal:
one should assign Ḍākinī to the east, and likewise Rāmā to the north.
Khaṇḍarohā is in the west, while Rūpiṇī is in the south;
she is blue, yellow, red, and green as the fourth.
She has four faces, eight arms, and three eyes; she possesses fierce splendor, sits in the half-lotus posture, has loose hair, and is enchanting.
Naked, wearing garlands of severed heads, and adorned with the five mudrās;
they hold skull-cups, khaṭvāṅga staffs, hand-drums, bells, and flaying knives.
Likewise, they bear arrows and the Gāṇḍīva bow, with hands like thunderbolts and heroes; they perform beautiful dances with the brandishing of their arms, swaying with passionate compassion.
Blue, yellow, green, and black, with hair standing erect.
The first [face] is yellow, blue, green, and red, with its upper face terrifying; the second is red, blue, and green, while its upper face is white and peaceful;
the third has a green, red, blue, and yellow upper face.
Trampled by the four Māras, gazing at the face of the Blessed One,
there are vases filled with the nectar of primordial wisdom in the corner sections.
Externally, there is a most beautiful peaked pavilion containing the commitment of the three wheels;
Gaurī is in the east and Caurī is in the north.
Pramohā is in the west, Vetālī in the south,
and Pokkasī likewise in the southeast.
In the southwest is Caṇḍālī,
in the northwest is Ghasmarī, and likewise in the northeast is the eighth, Herukābhā.
Gaurī is yellow, blue, and green;
Caurī is red, blue, and green;
Pramohā is blue, yellow, and green.
Vetālī is white, blue, and green;
Pukkasī is multicolored, red, blue, and green;
Caṇḍālī is green, blue, and yellow.
Ghasmarī is smoke-colored, blue, and green;
Herukābhā is blue, white, and red.
All of these have three eyes, loose hair, and are naked, dancing while standing upon corpses.
Adorned with the five mudrās, holding a khaṭvāṅga, skull-cup, bell, hand-drum, noose, and goad, and wearing garlands of skulls;
all have Akṣobhya as their crest-jewel.
Thus, she resides in the sacred seats and secondary seats, bestowing all accomplishments.
Thus, in the mind-cakras, Gaurī and the others are considered to be the yoginīs.
When served, they will grant even unattained accomplishments;
one attains the state of a Khecarī and succeeds as a divine Khecarī.
Then, on the outer speech-wheel,
there is a lute in the east, signified by the gesture of a lute, and a flute in the north, signified by the gesture of a flute.
In the west, Mṛdaṅgā by means of the gesture of a mṛdaṅga drum;
in the south, Murajā by means of the gesture of a muraja drum;
[they are] blue, yellow, red, and green.
In the southeast and other directions are Vajrahāsyā,
Vajralāsyā, and Vajragītā.
Vajranṛtyā is red, yellow, blue, and green.
These [deities] have one face, four arms, are naked, with disheveled hair, and wear garlands of skulls.
Dancing, three-eyed, and bearing skull-cups and *khaṭvāṅga* staffs,
they perform gestures of brandishing hands, the gestures of the vajra and bell, the sounding of cymbals, and the whirling of lotuses;
these reside in the fields, sub-fields, *cchanda*, and *upacchanda*.
They wear crowns featuring Amitābha.
In the body wheel,
flowers are in the east and incense in the north.
In the west are lamps, and in the south are perfumes;
they are yellow, smoky-colored, red, and white.
The mirror has taste and touch as its properties.
In the southeast and other directions, they are white as the moon, red, white, and green;
these goddesses have three eyes, loose hair, and are naked, dancing with their feet raised and their hands occupied with worship.
They carry skull-bowls and khaṭvāṅgas, hold hand-drums (*ḍamaru*) in their hands, and wear garlands of skulls.
One should meditate on these goddesses, who abide in the meeting places, intermediate meeting places, cremation grounds, and intermediate cremation grounds,
and who wear Vairocana upon their crowns.
At the gates are Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajrapāśa, and Vajrasphoṭa.
Vajrāveśā is blue, green, red, and yellow;
she is located in the east, north, west, and south corners, starting from the southeast.
Yamadāḍhī and the others are red, blue, smoke-colored, and yellow; they hold a skull, a khaṭvāṅga, their own respective emblems, and a ḍamaru drum.
Holding a flaying knife and a severed head, three-eyed, with disheveled hair and naked, they stand in a dancing posture;
all are adorned with the five mudrās and wear garlands of skulls, their crowns bearing the lords of their respective families, stationed in due order.

Having visualized within his heart the triad of wheels of body, speech, and mind of the Jñānasattva, and having visualized [the deity] together with the sovereign white, red, and blue Vīrayoginī as established according to the oral instructions,

one should meditate on drawing in the wheel of gnosis with the hook of gnosis, worshiping it, consecrating it in due order, and then, becoming one with it in a single fusion, perform the transformation.
Having cultivated [the practice] in due order and exerted effort in the recitation of the mantra that generates knowledge,
one should maintain [the concentration] precisely through the sequence of touching, exhilarating, and breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Reciting "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ" in this sequence,
one should perform it without counting until fatigue arises;
thereafter, being composed in meditation, one should perform the recitation of the *samaya* wheel.
One should recite the supreme vow using a rosary of large beads.

Having purified the eye according to the rule, one should always recite [the mantra] with the food-restriction rule,
joined with the yoga of the inner self by means of wisdom and skillful means.

Through union with the consort who is one's own means (*upāya*), there flashes forth the emanation of the Wrathful One, whose nature is non-dual equality and who has brought the three worlds to completion.
Having manifested the form of Heruka throughout the entire threefold world,
he shall cause all beings to enter therein and sport with their body, speech, and mind.
By this application of the ritual method, one should recite through the contemplation of the action;
by union with one's own tutelary deity, one perceives the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
At the time of the moment of arising, all the Tathāgatas, Vīras, Yoginīs,
and Ḍākinīs entreat Surata-krodha for that bliss.
And they serve, relying on enjoyments, with delight through the practice of entering into bliss.
O Rama! O abode of bliss! O supreme joy of great yoga!
O lotus-like bliss of the supreme Yogini!
Alala-laha!
O Suragha, supreme bliss! May my net of excellent yoginīs be perfected;
may the Ācārya come.
Ascend [to heaven] without me; let the bliss of the gods be yours.
Give me a net of excellent jewels.
This is the eye of Viṣayaṇa.
Great bliss is liberation; bliss is the characteristic of liberation. Bliss indeed, bliss indeed—suffering is not found there.
Liberation is bliss; the excellent quality spreads forth like a lotus.
O best of bees, abandon this body born of the lower realm;
let great bliss come, and let the sound of joy and the cry of "Sasiya" arise upon your chest.
Urged by this [song], the Lord Śaśimaṇḍala,
filled with longing through the spring passion, began to sing in sweet tones.
One should demonstrate all activities through the stainless timing of the ḍākinīs;
one should unite with all siddhis within the delightful vajra-lotus.
And by this, when employed at the proper time by the Vajra-holder who is joined with Kalā-vajra and impelled by passion, he bestows great bliss.
At the beginning, middle, and end, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra for the stabilization of the wheel of heroes among the ḍākinīs.
For all mantras, for all wrathful deities, and for all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, there will be a firm establishment of that which is hidden within their hearts.

Oṃ vajraheruka, protect the samaya! Arise as Heruka; be firm for me! Be devoted to me; be well-pleased with me; be well-nourished by me! Grant me all accomplishments; make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ! O Blessed One Vajraheruka, do not abandon me! Be Vajraheruka, the Great Samayasattva! Āḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus, the Blessed One, the Lord of a Hundred Syllables, who is all-pervasive, is himself manifest as Vajraheruka-Pratyaṅgirā; these are to be placed upon the sixteen petals.
One should solidify one’s own person as the maṇḍala of the previous instruction; possessing the yoga of one’s own presiding deity, one should dwell at ease and perceive the triple world.
The yogi should meditate upon such a stainless existence;
one who possesses such [realization] becomes a master of urine and should contemplate that which is established within the self.

No vow has been prescribed for him, nor a rosary, nor the recitation of mantras; there is no practice of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) or fire-offerings (homa), according to the sequence of the ritual procedure for the Āsphāṇaka.

There is no performance of mudrās or yogic practice involving the stepping out in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; the Great Vajra, which is to be grasped through meditative cultivation, is itself the creator of emanation.
One should perform the cessation [of breath] and also worship externally;
one should meditate on the full moon mandala in the center of the navel.
Therein, one should contemplate the syllable situated in the center, the supreme state;
one should meditate on the form of the deity as the union of body, speech, and mind.
For him, there is that which transcends the physical body, and he should not even cultivate the mind;
there is neither passion nor dispassion, for by reason it is called "dispassion."
One should honor the middle [deity], who resides in the heart-lotus and is not perceived as a resting place,
as "all women," for she is born from the Citta-vajra and is the Yoginīs.
It is thus called the Supreme Mudrā, adorned with fifty [letters] above the moon;
it is the unsurpassed gnosis, the supreme mind, because it is free from discursive thought.
Having thus rested in that state— which is beyond the mind, attained through the path of the guru’s instruction, and characterized by manifold light—
one must effect the absolute union and separation [of the winds]; this is the state of solitary liberation.
In this way, enlightenment would be extremely difficult to attain and is considered to be fruitless.
For a man of inferior intellect who follows other methods, such as the teachings of false heretics or the Prabhāsvara [meditation], his practice is fruitless despite his efforts.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the sequence of the seats of body, speech, and mind, in the Abhidhānottara.
